title: Will a universal catalytic converter set off the check engine light on an Infiniti G35?

# Will a universal catalytic converter set off the check engine light on an Infiniti G35?

Your 2004 Infiniti G35 is currently throwing a diagnostic trouble code (DTC) for the bank 2 catalytic converter efficiency. You are considering swapping the OEM unit, which is California compliant, with a universal Magnaflow replacement that is 49-state compliant. The immediate concern is whether this hardware change will persistently trigger the check engine light, causing an automatic emissions failure in Colorado.

The short answer is yes. If you install a universal converter on a vehicle originally equipped with a specific California-compliant unit, the check engine light will almost certainly illuminate and stay on. This behavior is not a malfunction of your Infiniti's engine control module (ECM); it is a direct result of how the OBD-II system validates catalytic efficiency against baseline expectations.

When you drive the car, the ECM continuously monitors oxygen sensor data before and after the converter. Specifically, it looks at the downstream oxygen sensor to determine if the catalyst is effectively storing oxygen and smoothing out exhaust pulses. A functioning converter creates a specific "rich-to-lean" oscillation pattern that the ECM expects based on the factory calibration maps stored in its flash memory.

Universal converters often lack the precise thermal mass and catalytic substrate geometry required to mimic this exact sensor signature. Even if the universal part works efficiently enough to reduce actual emissions (which is why they are sold), the downstream oxygen sensor may detect a different response time or amplitude than what the ECM's lookup tables anticipate. The system interprets this discrepancy as a catalyst efficiency drop below 85% and stores the P0420 code.

The distinction between "CA compliant" and "49-state compliant" is legally significant but technically irrelevant to the light staying on. Both types are designed to reduce emissions, but the CA-compliant unit was tuned specifically for the G35's emissions calibration. The 49-state universal unit, while functional, does not match the OEM hardware parameters the ECM uses to validate performance.

You mentioned that Magnaflow offers an exact replacement that is also 49-state compliant for approximately $600. Even though this part matches the physical dimensions and flow characteristics of the original, it still carries a non-CO certification label. In Colorado, where emissions testing is strict, using any component that is not specifically certified for that state can lead to rejection during the inspection. The inspector will likely see the "49-state" sticker or lack a specific CO approval stamp and fail the vehicle regardless of whether the check engine light is off.

If your primary goal is to turn off the light without legal compliance issues, you must replace the unit with one that carries the exact same California certification as the original part. The universal options, despite their lower cost, introduce a fundamental mismatch between the physical hardware and the software calibration. This mismatch forces the ECM into a fail-safe mode where it prevents further drive cycles or maintains the active DTC to ensure the vehicle does not operate in an unverified emissions state.

In summary, swapping to a universal converter will result in a persistent check engine light because the downstream oxygen sensor readings will deviate from the factory-calibrated expectations. To resolve the issue legitimately in Colorado, you need a replacement part that matches both the physical specifications and the specific emissions certification of your original unit.
